segments.title: Why the Royal Navy might have built Tiger Cubs
segments.body: The Tiger Cub counterfactual brings forward a cruiser purchase judged likely in 1914 or 1915 to 1912. Battlecruisers were becoming too expensive to provide in the numbers required for worldwide presence, while Britain already had 9.2-inch gun expertise and manufacturers willing to improve the weapon. Earlier orders would fill the gap before the war. Political reluctance to ask for another class while armored cruisers and early battlecruisers remained in service is the proposed explanation for the delay.

evidence.note: Cruiser procurement gap, political cost of another class, and continued British development of 9.2-inch guns.

segments.summary: A plausible 1912 procurement choice puts 9.2-inch cruisers between increasingly costly battlecruisers and the light cruisers needed for worldwide service.

segments.title: Gun selection was also an industrial policy
segments.body: Royal Navy choices between the 13.5-inch and 14-inch guns show why the nominally best weapon was not always the best fleet purchase. A gun supported by several barrel and ammunition makers protected the Navy from monopoly dependence and created competition for recurring practice and wartime orders. Practice firing made ammunition supply a continuing annual commitment rather than a one-time procurement choice. Continued private development of 9.2-inch guns therefore suggests that manufacturers expected a plausible future naval market even when no new cruiser class had yet been ordered.

evidence.note: Single-source 14-inch production was less resilient than the broader 13.5-inch supply base, while continued private work on 9.2-inch guns suggested an expected future market.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy preferred weapons that several firms could supply, making barrels and ammunition an industrial-resilience question as well as a performance choice.

segments.title: Battlecruiser evolution made numbers unaffordable
segments.body: Armor thickness alone does not define a ship's type. Coverage and internal subdivision determine how much of the ship can survive a hit, placing armored cruisers, battlecruisers, fast battleships, and dreadnought battleships along a spectrum. Early battlecruisers could replace armored cruisers at tolerable cost. Later ships such as HMS Tiger were too valuable and too few to serve routinely as station flagships or convoy escorts, leaving room for a cheaper 9.2-inch cruiser.

evidence.note: From armoured cruisers through battlecruisers to fast battleships, greater armour coverage, subdivision, capability, and cost reduced the number of ships a fleet could afford.

segments.summary: The progression from armored cruisers through battlecruisers to fast battleships increased armor coverage, subdivision, capability, and cost.

segments.title: Station flagships made naval deterrence scalable
segments.body: The Royal Navy used sloops and light cruisers for routine presence, then relied on a station flagship to deliver a more serious warning when a dispute escalated. That ship showed that a local squadron, and ultimately a battle squadron from the home or Mediterranean fleet, could follow if the warning was ignored. Armored cruisers also reinforced fleets and protected important convoys in wartime, so the role demanded both capability and numbers. A larger battlecruiser could outgrow a station's yards and ports or make its arrival a stronger threat than the dispute required. As HMS Tiger-type battlecruisers became second-rate capital assets and older cruisers approached retirement, a cheaper 9.2-inch cruiser could restore the missing third-rate mass.

evidence.note: Station-flagship deterrence, wartime escort duties, and the declining supply of affordable ships as battlecruisers grew.

segments.summary: Armored cruisers supplied an intermediate rung between routine flag-showing patrols and the arrival of a battle squadron, but later battlecruisers became too scarce and expensive for that work.

segments.title: A 28-knot station cruiser and technology test bed
segments.body: The proposed ship sits between 6,000-ton light cruisers and 28,000-ton HMS Tiger and could be built by more yards in larger batches. Six to eight 9.2-inch guns and a designed speed of 28 knots give it enough power to deter a raider without the cost of a capital ship. Small-tube boilers would let the Navy test machinery with less risk than fitting it first to a battleship; station service remained useful if the experiment disappointed. A successful installation might also influence the later R class. Its planned jobs include station flagship, convoy escort, reconnaissance, and fast support for the fleet.

evidence.note: Proposed displacement, armament, boiler trials, available building capacity, and overseas station duties.
The 28-knot requirement matches the fleet's reconnaissance cruisers and HMS Tiger.

segments.summary: The proposed Tiger Cub combines six to eight 9.2-inch guns, turbine machinery, and 28-knot speed in a 15,000- to 18,000-ton station cruiser.

segments.title: A convoy escort can deter a stronger raider through damage
segments.body: A Tiger Cub could protect a convoy by making an attack too costly for a stronger raider. Its aim would be to damage a battlecruiser enough for the next British ship to catch and defeat it. A raider expecting to win the immediate fight would still have to consider whether that victory ended its wider operation. This requirement helps explain the 9.2-inch battery: it provides a credible threat without the expense and weight of capital-ship guns.

evidence.note: A convoy escort deters a stronger raider by threatening damage that would make a later encounter fatal.
The 9.2-inch gun balances cruiser fighting ranges and installation demands with the ability to damage an attacking battlecruiser during convoy defence.

segments.summary: An escort does not have to defeat a battlecruiser alone if the damage it inflicts would leave the raider vulnerable to the next British warship.

segments.title: The Mark XII's promise and the limits of monitor gun trials
segments.body: The Mark X offered dependable barrel life, while the longer Mark XI wore out too quickly to be the preferred choice. The Mark XII restored barrel life and offered better range, but its availability for a 1912 order remains an inference from an approximate 1913 date and earlier development work. Its recorded ranges came from monitor mountings elevated to 40 degrees. Those results suggest useful fire out to about 18,000 yards in a cruiser installation, against expected cruiser engagements below 13,000 yards. The comparison uses about two rounds per minute, although the Mark XII's rate and barrel-life evidence also come from monitor conditions. A cruiser mounting's performance would therefore need to be estimated. Lighter ammunition and turret machinery than a 12-inch weapon would help keep the proposed ship affordable.

evidence.note: Mark X, XI, and XII range and barrel-life comparisons, monitor-derived performance figures, and expected cruiser engagement distances.

segments.summary: The Mark XII offers a plausible balance of range, barrel life, and installation weight, with its 1912 availability and cruiser performance inferred from limited evidence.

segments.title: Cruisers as technology trials and command schools
segments.body: Britain's large industrial base allowed cruiser construction to spread risk across multiple hulls and yards. An unsuccessful feature could still earn useful service on a quiet station, whereas a successful one could migrate into capital ships. The class would also create more commands in which officers could practice high-speed maneuver, fire control, and gunnery before moving into the battlecruiser force. Those posts mattered because the naval race kept the existing battlecruisers concentrated in European waters instead of serving as worldwide training commands. More experience might also change battlecruiser gunnery practices, although the scenario cannot establish that officers would make different decisions.

evidence.note: Cruisers provide affordable technology trials and additional training commands for fast-ship officers.

segments.summary: A numerous cruiser class could test machinery for battleships and give captains and gunnery officers experience handling large fast ships.

segments.title: Why Tiger Cubs still needed quick-firing secondary guns
segments.body: The proposed design carries triple 4-inch mountings as a quick-firing secondary battery rather than treating the main armament as sufficient for every threat. These were open-backed mounts, despite the enclosed turrets shown by the design game's visual model. A fast cruiser conducting reconnaissance could unexpectedly meet coastal torpedo boats at short range. Rapid secondary fire therefore protects the ship in the kind of close, confused action for which its long-range 9.2-inch battery was not optimized.

evidence.note: Open-backed triple 4-inch mounts and their use against coastal torpedo boats during fast reconnaissance.

segments.summary: Triple 4-inch mounts give a fast reconnaissance cruiser the rapid fire needed when its large 9.2-inch guns are poorly suited to close encounters with torpedo boats.

segments.title: British yards and Dominion orders could create a large class
segments.body: Recent capital-ship yards, including Thames Ironworks, could take this work, and a continuing program might keep those facilities open. That spare capacity rested on roughly 150 years of consistent British investment in shipbuilding infrastructure, including the ability to enlarge facilities quickly when a program required it. Australia could pair these cruisers with HMAS Australia, while Canada and other Dominions might find them easier to finance, crew, and sustain than battleships. Four British ships per year plus two Dominion-funded orders per year could put as many as eighteen Tiger Cubs into production by 1914. Most foreign navies lacked the spare capacity for an immediate answer.

evidence.note: British yard capacity, retention of older ships, and possible Dominion-funded orders determine the available building program.

segments.summary: Four British ships per year plus possible Australian, Canadian, New Zealand, or Malayan orders could place as many as eighteen Tiger Cubs in production by 1914.

segments.title: How a large navy assigns first-, second-, and tertiary-line duties
segments.body: Wartime naval employment falls into first-, second-, and tertiary-line duties. First-line ships handle the primary fleet battles, while second-line forces escort convoys and patrol waters where surface raiders may appear. Tertiary work includes troop transport, amphibious support, counter-piracy, and maintaining a presence in regions that remain quiet only because a warship is there. New Tiger Cubs would not automatically release every older cruiser for disposal once war began, since even obsolete combatants could free modern ships from necessary low-threat tasks.

evidence.note: Tertiary, second-line, and first-line duties help explain why the wartime Navy retained old ships.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy retained almost any serviceable hull in 1914 because major battle, convoy protection, and low-threat presence each demanded different levels of ship.

segments.title: Blücher shows what the Tiger Cub had to beat
segments.body: Blücher carried twelve 8.3-inch guns and could make about 25.4 knots, a formidable combination against older cruisers. A Tiger Cub with eight longer-ranged 9.2-inch guns and a designed speed of 28 knots could dictate the range. Turbine machinery and small-tube boilers might widen that service-speed advantage beyond the nominal 2.6 knots. Germany would therefore have to treat the new cruiser as more than a routine station ship even though it was not a capital ship.

evidence.note: Blücher's guns and speed against the proposed Tiger Cub's heavier armament, greater range, and turbine-powered speed advantage.

segments.summary: The German armored cruiser Blücher provides a concrete benchmark for the proposed British ship's speed, armament, and ability to control an engagement.

segments.title: American yard politics could reshape the Lexington program
segments.body: France and Italy had already committed their limited prewar construction capacity, while Germany was building a lopsided fleet. American politics offered a different mechanism. Charleston Navy Yard could build cruisers but not the historical Lexington-class battlecruisers, and Senator Benjamin Tillman had a constituency interest in restoring cruiser construction. With federal investment, a British Tiger Cub precedent might therefore redirect the American program toward a 9.2-inch or similar large cruiser that the yard could actually build.

evidence.note: Senator Benjamin Tillman's interest in cruiser work for Charleston Navy Yard, whose capacity was below the historical Lexington battlecruiser, could redirect federal investment toward an alternate large-cruiser design.

segments.summary: Senator Benjamin Tillman's interest in cruiser work for Charleston Navy Yard creates a possible American route from Lexington battlecruisers to large station cruisers.

segments.title: The qualitative naval race ran on shared technology
segments.body: Queen Elizabeth- and R-class costs had already pushed the German army and navy into a funding conflict that the navy was unlikely to win. Germany then faced a qualitative contest in which Britain, the United States, Japan, and Italy competed while also exchanging components and expertise. Parsons turbines and other British components formed part of several rival fleets' industrial base. A numerous 28-knot cruiser that could reinforce British battlecruisers would deepen German insecurity without requiring Britain to add another formal capital-ship type.

evidence.note: Germany's shift from quantity to quality, technology exchange among rival navies, and the added pressure of fast British 9.2-inch cruisers.

segments.summary: Tiger Cub construction would add pressure as Germany left the quantitative race, while Britain and several competitors improved ships through overlapping industrial networks.

segments.title: Two Tiger Cubs could reverse the Battle of Coronel
segments.body: Two newly commissioned Tiger Cubs could reinforce Rear Admiral Christopher Cradock in the South Atlantic. Their sixteen 9.2-inch guns, modern fire control, and 28-knot speed would outmatch Scharnhorst and Gneisenau. Cradock would probably transfer his flag and combine the Tiger Cubs with Glasgow in a fast division, leaving Good Hope, Monmouth, and Otranto in a slower group. A British victory could still cost ships if the Germans engaged that slower group before help arrived, although contemporary radio limits would discourage separating the divisions widely. Victory at Coronel would remove the need to send Invincible and Inflexible south for the Falklands battle. The Tiger Cubs would gain the public reputation for destroying raiders, while the battlecruisers would lose the victory that historically answered criticism after Goeben escaped.

evidence.note: Two Tiger Cubs could reverse the firepower and speed balance at Coronel. Separate fast and slow divisions would still leave a risk of British losses before the faster ships intervened.

segments.summary: Sixteen 9.2-inch guns and a major speed advantage would transform Cradock's force against Scharnhorst and Gneisenau.

segments.title: Could the Tiger Cubs have revived the frigate name?
segments.body: Station cruiser sounded dull, medium cruiser carried awkward period meanings, and dreadnought cruiser risked confusion with battlecruisers. Officers such as Jellicoe regarded 'large light cruiser' as political wordplay that said little about a warship's role. John Fisher had already returned the word frigate to discussion, making it a possible name for these ships. Heavy and light frigate categories could then distinguish the 9.2-inch ships from smaller cruisers. During the Second World War, sloops used naval construction, corvettes stayed close to merchant practice, and twin-screw frigates occupied an intermediate position. Using frigate for a cruiser category earlier could leave the later anti-submarine escort needing a different name.

evidence.note: Station cruiser and dreadnought cruiser naming, and objections to the politically convenient but uninformative phrase large light cruiser.
Heavy and light frigate names for cruisers, followed by the later distinction between naval-built sloops, merchant-style corvettes, and twin-screw frigates.

segments.summary: Contemporary naming debates make frigate a plausible label for a medium 9.2-inch cruiser between light cruisers and battlecruisers.

segments.title: Cradock's survival could improve British fleet reporting
segments.body: Victory at Coronel allows Christopher Cradock to survive and return to Britain with the Tiger Cub squadron. The counterfactual places him under David Beatty as a deputy commander of the fast forces. Cradock's South Atlantic staff regularly sent relevant updates even when senior authorities did not always act on them. If Jellicoe encouraged that reporting habit, the Grand Fleet might receive earlier and clearer information about the German fleet during a Jutland-type encounter.

evidence.note: Cradock's possible return as Beatty's deputy and his staff's habit of sending regular, relevant reports.
Cradock's reports could help Jellicoe bring the Grand Fleet south in time for a Jutland encounter.

segments.summary: A victorious Christopher Cradock could return as a fast-squadron deputy whose staff's habit of sending regular reports gives Jellicoe better information in later fleet actions.

segments.title: Tiger Cubs displace Fisher's large light cruisers
segments.body: A victory at Coronel would provide the Royal Navy with a clear wartime narrative. It still would not save Prince Louis of Battenberg from the political campaign against him. Fisher would return to office without a persuasive need for his large light cruisers because the Tiger Cubs already supply fast Baltic-capable ships in quantity. Renown and Repulse might still win approval as 15-inch battlecruisers intended to meet Germany's next generation. Small-tube boilers could already have raised the Revenge class toward Queen Elizabeth speeds. If redesign interrupted construction, the remaining three R-class ships might instead become battlecruisers, adding Resistance to Renown and Repulse.

evidence.note: Battenberg's political vulnerability, the weakened case for the Courageous class, and possible small-tube-boiler changes to the R-class and battlecruiser programs.

segments.summary: An established 9.2-inch cruiser program weakens the case for Courageous, Glorious, and Furious and may reshape the Renown and R-class programs.

segments.title: Why the Royal Navy needed visible wartime victories
segments.body: The Royal Navy performed indispensable but often invisible work throughout the First World War. That diffuse contribution was harder to explain than the Western Front's continuous and highly visible mass involvement. A clear victory at Coronel would let the service show how a battle enabled command of the sea rather than merely asserting that command existed. That narrative would strengthen the Navy's case for wartime construction and its position in later arguments over budgets and institutional priorities.

evidence.note: The Navy's difficulty creating a visible wartime narrative and the institutional value of a Coronel victory.

segments.summary: A Tiger Cub victory at Coronel would give the Navy a simple public story linking sea control to funding, institutional survival, and future investment.

segments.title: Tiger Cubs turn Dogger Bank into a German disaster
segments.body: The fast British battlecruisers could pursue with Tiger Cub support while slower ships formed a second group. Cradock's cruiser command would provide another senior officer willing to continue the chase if Beatty's signals drew the battlecruisers toward Blücher. A recent independent victory at Coronel would also give Cradock more standing to exercise his own judgment. High rates of fire remain dangerous to unarmored control, deck, and superstructure areas even when 9.2-inch shells cannot defeat every belt. Seydlitz and Moltke are unlikely to escape in this counterfactual, while Derfflinger has the best chance because of her higher speed. The possible loss of Franz von Hipper with Seydlitz would deprive Germany of ships and experienced cruiser leadership before Jutland.

evidence.note: Additional British cruisers increase pursuit speed and firepower, threaten Seydlitz and Moltke, and create possible losses of German leadership and ammunition-handling lessons.

segments.summary: Four to six 28-knot cruisers add enough speed and 9.2-inch firepower to threaten the entire German scouting group rather than only Blucher.

segments.title: Fast squadrons need escorts that can keep up
segments.body: Lion and Princess Royal could make 27.5 knots, while Tiger and the proposed Tiger Cubs could reach 28. That gives the fast battlecruisers enough support to advance without waiting for the slower capital ships. The escort screen would also divide by speed: Southampton's official 25.5 knots would leave her behind, while enough of the Harwich Force could accompany the leading group. The First Light Cruiser Squadron could support the slower battlecruisers as the faster cruisers and destroyers pressed ahead. This arrangement would bring a stronger British force into contact sooner against German ships whose speed was limited by Blücher.

evidence.note: British capital-ship and escort speeds support separate pursuit and following groups, with the Harwich Force accompanying the faster ships.

segments.summary: Tiger Cubs let Lion, Princess Royal, and Tiger pursue together, while escort speeds determine which light cruisers and destroyers can accompany them.

segments.title: 9.2-inch fire could cripple what belt armour did not cover
segments.body: The counterfactual does not require each Tiger Cub to defeat a German battlecruiser alone. Dogger Bank's ranges fell inside the useful reach of the Mark XII 9.2-inch gun, and several cruisers could add a high volume of fire to the British battlecruisers' heavier salvos. Thick belt armour could not cover every control position, deck fitting, or part of the superstructure. Even high-explosive hits in those areas could start fires, disrupt fighting efficiency, and make escape harder for an already slower German force.

evidence.note: Dogger Bank's engagement ranges permit rapid 9.2-inch fire against vulnerable decks and superstructures outside the heaviest armour.

segments.summary: At Dogger Bank ranges, rapid 9.2-inch fire could damage battlecruiser control positions, decks, and superstructures even without penetrating the thickest armour belt.

segments.title: Dogger Bank could remove both German leaders and safety lessons
segments.body: If Seydlitz is sunk, Admiral Franz von Hipper may die with her only months after Maximilian von Spee is lost at Coronel. Germany would then lose two of its most experienced senior officers in cruiser warfare before the decisive 1916 campaign. The historical Seydlitz survived Dogger Bank and exposed dangerous magazine and ammunition-handling practices that the High Seas Fleet could correct. In this counterfactual, that lesson may vanish with the ship, while a heavily damaged British survivor could instead give the Royal Navy its own warning.

evidence.note: Hipper's possible death would worsen the shortage of experienced German cruiser commanders, while losing Seydlitz could prevent ammunition-handling reforms before Jutland.

segments.summary: Losing Admiral Hipper and Seydlitz would deprive Germany of experienced cruiser command and the damage evidence that historically prompted safer ammunition handling before Jutland.

segments.title: Pursuit and interception in the Dogger Bank simulations
segments.body: Derfflinger escapes in about 40 percent of the computer runs of this counterfactual. In the remaining runs, British losses range from two Tiger Cubs to two Tiger Cubs and a battlecruiser, often Princess Royal. Total German losses usually occur when the fast British group drives the retreating ships into the slower group, which has moved onto an interception course. The extra cruisers support the pursuit while the slower ships block the German withdrawal.

evidence.note: Derfflinger escapes in about 40 percent of the computer runs. Complete German losses usually involve interception by the slower British group and cost two Tiger Cubs, sometimes with a battlecruiser.

segments.summary: Repeated computer runs leave Derfflinger able to escape in roughly 40 percent of cases, while total German losses usually require the fast British group to drive the retreating ships into a slower interception force.

segments.title: Global deployment without wasting battlecruisers
segments.body: A pair stationed with older battleships could catch and delay Goeben if she attempted to break out, while other ships could provide gunnery and command support at Gallipoli. Additional tactical firepower cannot repair a campaign already compromised at the strategic level. An Australian Tiger Cub might take on the visible national role that would be too costly for HMAS Australia, including evacuation duties that connect the navy directly with the Australian Imperial Force. By late 1915 the class offers enough hulls to cover distant commitments without stripping the battlecruiser force.

evidence.note: Cruiser interception of Goeben, Gallipoli fire support, Australian evacuation duties, and deployment of individual ships while retaining a concentrated force at home.

segments.summary: Numerous fast cruisers can guard against Goeben, support Gallipoli, and reinforce distant stations while a concentrated squadron remains with the Grand Fleet.

segments.title: Why more cruiser firepower does not solve Gallipoli
segments.body: Fast 9.2-inch cruisers could improve fire support at Gallipoli and operate closer inshore than a battleship, but they would not correct the campaign's strategic failure. A much more radical proposal would pack and seal the forward and outer spaces of old Royal Sovereign-type battleships with cork, add large bulges, and use them to force a path through the minefields. Surviving warships could then reach Constantinople with troopships close behind, aiming to capture the Ottoman cabinet and dictate peace terms. Such a plan is considered unlikely to be attempted. A more plausible role for an Australian Tiger Cub would be to evacuate the last Australian troops, giving the navy a direct place in the national memory of Gallipoli.

evidence.note: Extra Tiger Cubs could improve fire support and an Australian evacuation. The separate, unlikely plan to force the Dardanelles uses modified old battleships and following troopships.

segments.summary: Tiger Cubs could improve local fire control and evacuation, though only a radically different operational concept could overcome Gallipoli's strategic failure.

segments.title: Earlier victories transform the balance at Jutland
segments.body: Germany reaches 1916 with fewer battlecruisers, no Hipper, and a scouting group badly outmatched by British battlecruisers, the Fifth Battle Squadron, and perhaps ten or twelve Tiger Cubs. Removing two battlecruisers at Dogger Bank would strip roughly 40 percent of the five-ship German scouting group present at historical Jutland. Better reporting from Cradock could give Jellicoe earlier information while the slower German battle fleet tries to protect its damaged scouts. The outcome ranges from an early German withdrawal to a full meeting engagement in which the Grand Fleet accepts serious losses to destroy the High Seas Fleet.

evidence.note: Changed scouting forces, leadership, communications, fleet speeds, and possible Jutland outcomes.
Two lost battlecruisers amount to 40 percent of the historical German scouting group's Jutland strength, compounding Britain's existing superiority.

segments.summary: German losses at Dogger Bank plus Tiger Cub squadrons make the British fast wing overwhelming and may expose the High Seas Fleet to annihilation.

segments.title: The German plan depended on defeating the Royal Navy in detail
segments.body: The High Seas Fleet could not seek a straightforward fleet action against the larger Royal Navy. Its operational logic required finding a detached British force, destroying it, withdrawing, and repeating the process until the numerical balance became favorable. Japan's later Kantai Kessen concept used similar attrition before a decisive engagement with the U.S. fleet. Tiger Cub squadrons undermine the German plan because even Britain's fast detached wing may appear as strong as the entire German force, removing the smaller target on which the strategy depends.

evidence.note: Germany's defeat-in-detail plan seeks isolated British forces before the fleet can concentrate, paralleling Japanese decisive-battle doctrine.

segments.summary: Germany needed to isolate and destroy smaller British formations repeatedly, a logic compared with Japan's later plan to reduce the U.S. fleet before a decisive battle.

segments.title: Jellicoe turned the Grand Fleet into a gunnery instrument
segments.body: A successful interception would still be costly, though the Grand Fleet held a training advantage. Jellicoe combined a gunnery emphasis comparable to U.S. Admiral Willis Lee with a strategic approach comparable to Andrew Cunningham's. The northern fleet's constrained existence gave crews repeated opportunities for gun drill and fire-control practice. British hit totals at Jutland therefore matter to the counterfactual: with better shells or a longer engagement, disciplined shooting could turn numerical superiority into the destruction of the High Seas Fleet.

evidence.note: Jellicoe's gunnery emphasis is compared with Willis Lee's and his strategic approach with Cunningham's. Daily Grand Fleet practice and British hits at Jutland support the possible outcome of a longer battle.

segments.summary: Daily practice under Jellicoe made British hitting power a central factor in any prolonged meeting engagement with the High Seas Fleet.

segments.title: Tiger Cub hulls could accelerate British carrier development
segments.body: Without Furious, Courageous, and Glorious available as experiments, Britain might apply Hermes-style carrier work to a Tiger Cub hull sooner. A carrier based on the cruiser hull could reach about 28 knots and carry roughly thirty to forty aircraft, offering a practical platform for reconnaissance and strike experiments. Several such ships might dash forward under a fast cruiser screen, launch torpedo aircraft against the German fleet at Wilhelmshaven, and withdraw before slower German units could respond. Early aerial torpedoes would remain unreliable, so the strike is a possibility rather than an assured result.

evidence.note: A larger, faster Hermes-like carrier could support a torpedo strike on Wilhelmshaven.

segments.summary: Without Furious, Courageous, and Glorious, a fast 15,000-ton Tiger Cub hull offers an alternative route to larger Hermes-type aircraft carriers.

segments.title: Why early aerial torpedoes might still threaten Wilhelmshaven
segments.body: British work on buoyancy, longer fins, and tension cables sought a controlled shallow entry for air-dropped torpedoes attacking ships in harbour. Wilhelmshaven's depth reduced the danger that a diving weapon would simply strike the bottom. The counterfactual allows perhaps twenty weapons from a sixty-torpedo strike to run correctly and roughly fifteen to hit. Ships considered safe in port might have many crew members ashore and internal doors open, making a modest number of hits disproportionately damaging.

evidence.note: British torpedo-entry experiments, Wilhelmshaven's depth, estimated weapon reliability, and relaxed harbour precautions. The torpedo-net wording is unclear in the captions.

segments.summary: British experiments with torpedo entry and a large surprise strike could make even unreliable early weapons dangerous against ships treating Wilhelmshaven as a safe anchorage.

segments.title: A destroyed High Seas Fleet opens the Baltic
segments.body: With the High Seas Fleet destroyed, fast cruisers could enter the Baltic, bombard the coast, and symbolize a new blockade, while submarines would perform much of the practical work of closing German imports. The surface fleet could also run supplies toward St Petersburg and provide a visible demonstration that Germany had lost command of the sea. That victory would give the Royal Navy a much stronger claim to having won the war and undermine any later argument that Germany's armed forces remained undefeated. An end in late 1916 would also precede American entry and avoid much of Britain's historically severe 1917-18 debt and battlefield loss.

evidence.note: Destruction of the High Seas Fleet permits a proposed Baltic blockade and Russian supply route, with possible consequences for peace timing and British finances.

segments.summary: If Jutland becomes a battle of annihilation, Britain can enter the Baltic, tighten the blockade, support Russia, and perhaps force peace in 1916.

segments.title: Why ending the war in 1916 transforms British finances
segments.body: The economic consequence of an earlier peace depends on when Britain financed each stage of the war. The financial sequence begins with 1914 and 1915 consuming accumulated reserves, while sales or pledges of other assets carried the country through 1916 and into 1917. The sharpest debt growth came in 1917 and 1918, together with postwar borrowing for recovery. A naval victory that forced peace in late 1916 would shorten the casualty lists and remove the most damaging borrowing years, leaving Britain in a markedly stronger postwar financial position.

evidence.note: Britain first uses reserves, then asset sales or pledges, before wartime debt surges later.

segments.summary: Britain first consumed financial reserves, then sold or pledged assets, and only later entered the steep debt phase associated with 1917 and 1918.

segments.title: A victory of annihilation could consume Britain's future admirals
segments.body: The proposed battle of annihilation could deliver strategic victory at an enormous price. The scenario allows for as much as a third of the British fleet being sunk, with additional ships returning severely damaged. Such losses would remove many officers whose names are familiar from the Royal Navy's later Second World War leadership. An earlier peace and healthier national finances would improve Britain's ability to rebuild, though they could not restore that lost generation of experience.

evidence.note: A third of the British fleet might be sunk, removing officers who otherwise become familiar from the Second World War.

segments.summary: Destroying the High Seas Fleet might cost Britain a third of its own fleet and erase officers who otherwise become familiar Royal Navy leaders in the Second World War.

segments.title: Tiger Cubs rewrite postwar cruiser and treaty categories
segments.body: The Hawkins class loses its rationale because Tiger Cubs already provide a faster and more heavily armed answer to distant raiders. If the war still produces a Washington-style conference, negotiators cannot leave unlimited 20,000-ton cruisers outside capital-ship limits without making 35,000-ton battleships uneconomic. One possible treaty scheme sets separate limits for light cruisers, the new frigate or heavy-cruiser category, carriers, and larger capital ships. Britain and the United States receive roughly comparable allocations, while Japan accepts a lower ratio.

evidence.note: Tiger Cubs displace the Hawkins requirement and introduce a 20,000-ton cruiser category into possible postwar arms limits.

segments.summary: An established 20,000-ton, 9.2-inch cruiser category displaces the Hawkins class and forces any arms treaty to regulate a powerful middle tier.

segments.title: An early peace could erase the Washington Naval Treaty
segments.body: A peace forced by naval victory in 1916 would occur before the United States entered the war or gained a place in the Versailles settlement. Britain would also see little reason to restrict a Royal Navy widely credited with winning the conflict. The postwar world is therefore too different for a Washington Naval Treaty to be the default outcome. Detailed treaty limits apply only to the alternate branch in which Germany retreats, the war continues, and American participation eventually recreates pressure for arms limitation.

evidence.note: An early peace would remove the presumed political basis for a Washington treaty, while the longer-war branch retains American entry and possible arms limits.

segments.summary: If the war ends in 1916 before American entry, the diplomatic coalition and political motive for a Washington-style naval settlement may never exist.

segments.title: A 20,000-ton cruiser changes every treaty category
segments.body: A treaty following the longer-war scenario would have to accommodate an established 20,000-ton cruiser category. Leaving those ships unrestricted would undermine a 35,000-ton capital-ship ceiling, since a navy could concentrate its resources on overwhelming cruiser numbers. One proposed settlement leaves ships up to 10,000 tons with 6- or possibly 7-inch guns unrestricted, then limits larger cruisers to 20,000 tons and 10-inch guns. Separate ceilings of about 30,000 tons for carriers and 40,000 tons for capital ships would regulate the larger categories. These are possible negotiating terms in the counterfactual branch where the war continues long enough to produce an arms-limitation conference.

evidence.note: Possible 10,000-, 20,000-, 30,000-, and 40,000-ton bands with distinct gun and numerical limits in a hypothetical postwar treaty.

segments.summary: Unrestricted Tiger Cub-sized cruisers would weaken a battleship limit, creating pressure for separate cruiser, carrier, and capital-ship ceilings.

segments.title: Existing cruisers and carrier duties shape fleet quotas
segments.body: Britain's existing Tiger Cubs would make a low large-cruiser quota difficult to accept. One possible agreement allows Britain and the United States twenty large cruisers, ten carriers, and fifteen battleships each. Japan might receive fourteen large cruisers, six carriers, and nine battleships, giving it 70 percent of the cruiser allowance and 60 percent in the other categories. Britain would also seek freedom to replace its experimental pre-treaty cruisers. Demand for ten carriers reflects reconnaissance, fleet information, and raider hunting as well as strike operations, so their value extends beyond the size of an attack force.

evidence.note: Possible British, American, and Japanese ship allowances, replacement rights for experimental cruisers, and carrier demand for reconnaissance and raider hunting.

segments.summary: Proposed British and American quotas reflect ships already built and the reconnaissance duties of carriers, with a higher Japanese ratio for large cruisers.

segments.title: A higher treaty ceiling permits faster British battleships
segments.body: A 40,000-ton ceiling would give Britain more room for machinery than the historical treaty settlement allowed. One proposal uses an F3-style arrangement with a longer hull, more shafts and boilers, and broadly comparable protection to produce a 28-knot ship at about 37,000 tons. The available tonnage might permit three such Nelson-type battleships. The same higher ceiling would also make a later King George V design with twelve 14-inch guns a plausible outcome.

evidence.note: An F3-style Nelson alternative with more machinery, about 37,000 tons, and a projected speed of 28 knots. The captioned gun-count phrase is unclear.
Three fast Nelson-type ships and twelve 14-inch guns for King George V under a higher treaty ceiling.

segments.summary: A 40,000-ton battleship ceiling could support three faster Nelson-type ships and a later King George V design with twelve 14-inch guns.

segments.title: Why a 10-inch treaty maximum could favour 9.2-inch guns
segments.body: A treaty maximum of 10 inches would tempt American and Japanese designers to use the largest permitted calibre. In this design comparison, 9.2-inch guns sit at the upper end of cruiser-grade turret machinery, while 10-inch shells demand heavier, capital-ship-style equipment. Britain could retain 9.2-inch guns to use its limited displacement more efficiently. A further Japanese possibility builds in the machinery needed for later 12-inch guns, but this would favour a six-gun arrangement because an eight-gun ship would be difficult to fit honestly within the limit.

evidence.note: Predicted American and Japanese interest in the maximum calibre and the machinery-weight argument for retaining British 9.2-inch guns.
A Japanese design allowing later 12-inch rearmament would probably need a six-gun layout.

segments.summary: Larger shells demand heavier turret machinery, potentially making 9.2-inch guns a better fit for a cruiser tonnage limit than the permitted 10-inch maximum.

segments.title: The missing third rate of the First World War
segments.body: Old armored cruisers and pre-dreadnoughts were nearing retirement, while modern battlecruisers were too scarce and costly to inherit all their work. A 9.2-inch station cruiser supplies the mass needed for deterrence, escort, distant presence, and reinforcement without demanding new capital-ship infrastructure. The likely explanation for postponing such a purchase is political restraint rather than a shortage of money, yards, guns, or crews. Without the war, the requirement probably returns in 1914 or 1915 as the older ships leave service.

evidence.note: A 9.2-inch cruiser could replace retiring station ships, with political restraint offered as the likely explanation for delaying procurement.

segments.summary: The Tiger Cub would supply the numerous, globally useful third-rate warship missing from the First World War fleet.

segments.title: The 'We Want Eight' compromise shows Admiralty leverage
segments.body: The 'We Want Eight' episode shows the strength of the Royal Navy's prewar political machine. The Admiralty wanted six ships and the Treasury preferred four, but a conditional compromise quickly produced eight once the stated trigger was met. Plans for the Queen Elizabeth and R classes likewise grew from nine ships to fourteen, showing that the government could be induced to fund major naval expansion. That total includes the projected Agincourt, whose nominal place in the 15-inch generation is qualified by the interpretation that she was intended to carry 18-inch guns. The argument for political restraint over Tiger Cubs therefore rests on whether another cruiser class was worth spending that political capital.

evidence.note: The 'We Want Eight' compromise and expansion of the Queen Elizabeth and R-class programs demonstrate Admiralty political leverage. The projected Agincourt's armament carries a separate 18-inch interpretation.

segments.summary: The dreadnought building campaign demonstrates why politics, rather than money or yards alone, best explains the absence of a Tiger Cub order.

segments.title: The Cressy losses still drive submarine caution
segments.body: Aboukir, Cressy, and Hogue would probably still be lost to a submarine in this scenario, preserving the Royal Navy's fear of underwater attack. Tiger Cubs would inherit more modern internal subdivision and organization from HMS Tiger's design era. Those features would improve their prospects of surviving a torpedo hit. The Navy could gain a more resilient cruiser force while retaining its historical operational caution about submarines.

evidence.note: The historical Cressy-class loss remains, while Tiger Cub cruisers likely have better subdivision and torpedo resilience.

segments.summary: Tiger Cubs would not save Aboukir, Cressy, and Hogue, but their newer subdivision might make the replacement cruiser force more resistant to torpedo damage.

segments.title: Interwar fleets adapt to a world full of Tiger Cubs
segments.body: A fleet of twenty or more Tiger Cub successors could concentrate against surface raiders far more quickly than the historical cruiser force. That reduces the appeal of Germany's Deutschland class because a raider could face several faster 9.2-inch cruisers rather than one widely dispersed response ship. Within a 400,000-ton allowance, twenty-two 18,000-ton cruisers might carry nine 9.2-inch guns apiece in three triple turrets. Higher treaty limits would also make faster British battleships possible, while American and Japanese cruiser designs would confront the extra weight of 10-inch armament. If a longer war still led to a naval treaty, unfinished Admiral-class battlecruisers could supply the carrier conversions otherwise associated with Courageous and Glorious. Those names might instead belong to 9.2-inch cruisers in this scenario.

evidence.note: Numerous 9.2-inch cruisers reduce the appeal of Deutschland-type raiders. Alternative treaty limits affect battleship and cruiser designs and could permit Admiral-class carrier conversions.

segments.summary: Numerous modern 9.2-inch cruisers make Deutschland-type raiders less compelling and push battleship and cruiser designs into different treaty tradeoffs.
